name: Ananas Reinette
summary: A small, crisp, juicy apple whose high-acid tang is balanced by plenty of sugar and a distinctive pineapple-like scent; some tasters find it almost sweet-shop in character. It grows sweeter as the skin deepens to gold but never loses its tang, and it makes a sharp, aromatic juice. The aroma is fullest after a warm summer.
best_eaten: Nov-Jan; keeps into February in a good store

name: Aport
summary: Grown in the Almaty foothills, the fine-grained flesh is crisp and sweet-tart at harvest with a strong honeyed scent, turning softer and crumbly in store. In Britain the same apple (as Emperor Alexander) is coarser, drier and much less flavoured, so climate makes a big difference.

name: Ashton Bitter
summary: A bittersweet with low acid and medium tannin, giving soft, mildly astringent juice. The flesh is fairly dry.
best_eaten: Not for eating; mill in Oct

name: Barnack Beauty
summary: Firm, very crisp, juicy creamy-white flesh with a sharp, tangy flavour tempered by some sweetness; not a sweet apple, and as useful for cooking as for eating. A sound late keeper rather than a perfumed one.

name: Belle de Pontoise
summary: Whitish, juicy flesh that is sweet with a clear tang; a late dessert apple that ripens in store around January and keeps for about five months.

name: Bethan
summary: A small, crisp, juicy and sweet early apple with more richness than most September fruit; the RHS fruit specialist Joan Morgan called it pretty and moreish.

name: Blue Pearmain
summary: Dense, very fine-grained flesh with a little crunch but no snap, moist rather than juicy. Sweet with a pear-like flavour and enough acid to leave a lingering tart finish; aromatic and substantial rather than refreshing. Keeps well in cold storage, though very old fruit turns rubbery.

name: Braintree Seedling
summary: Firm, fine-textured, crisp cream flesh with a sweet, aromatic flavour.

name: Butterball
summary: Mainly ornamental; the fruit is tart and is used for crab apple jelly rather than eaten.

name: Carswell's Orange
summary: Juicy, slightly coarse flesh with a pleasant aromatic flavour that shows its Cox parentage.

name: Chisel Jersey
summary: A full bittersweet: the juice is high in sugar and very high in tannin with little acid, giving heavy astringency and bitterness. Prized for body and mouthfeel in blends rather than for fresh eating.
best_eaten: Not for eating; mill in Nov-Dec after a short spell of sweating.

name: Colonel Vaughan
summary: Firm white flesh, sometimes stained with red, with a sweet to mildly acidic flavour.

name: Court Royal
summary: A true sweet cider apple: little acid and little tannin, so the juice is soft, sugary and plain, and it ferments quickly. The fruit is lightly crisp and sweet enough to eat fresh, which is why it once doubled as a dessert apple.
best_eaten: Oct-Nov; mill soon after picking, it does not need long sweating

name: Cripps Pink
summary: Very firm, fine-grained and crunchy with a refreshing, almost effervescent sharpness balanced by good sweetness. The acidity mellows in storage and the apple keeps its bite for months.
best_eaten: Dec-Apr; improves for a month or more after picking

name: Delbarestivale
summary: Aromatic and sweet with gentle acidity; juicy and fairly crisp for an early apple, and it keeps better than most summer varieties.

name: Dorsett Golden
summary: Sweet and fairly mild with a Golden Delicious character; lightly crisp and juicy. Flavour is said to be best on fruit ripened in light shade, and it softens quickly after picking.
best_eaten: Immediately after picking (Jun-Jul in subtropical climates)

name: Dunn's Favourite
summary: No verified tasting notes are available for this name.

name: Egremont Russet
summary: Dense cream flesh, moist rather than juicy, with a sweet, classically nutty flavour, a little balancing sharpness and a pear-like overtone that some tasters find marked. Crisp at picking, it grows sweeter and nuttier in store but also drier, eventually going woolly or shrivelled; good with cheese and in savoury salads.

name: Empire
summary: Crisp, crunchy, bright white flesh, juicy and sweet, with the vinous McIntosh character (likened to melon or elderflower) but less acidity. Best fresh from the tree, though it keeps into winter in a fridge and resists bruising; UK-grown or poorly stored fruit can be watery or mealy.

name: Fiesta
summary: Crisp, very juicy cream flesh with a sweet, Cox-like aromatic flavour backed by good acidity; some tasters pick up strawberry, and long-stored fruit can develop odd aniseed or brandy-like notes. Stays firm for months, though the sweetness fades; the skin is tough and the flesh holds firm when cooked. Good for juice.
best_eaten: Oct-Jan; best in the first two months

name: Freedom
summary: Crisp, very juicy cream flesh with a sweet, sprightly sub-acid flavour that some liken to McIntosh; pleasant rather than intense. It softens and turns mealy soon after picking, so eat it quickly or use it for sauce, drying, juice and cider.

name: Gascoyne's Scarlet
summary: Firm, fine-grained, rather dry white flesh, sweet with only a light, faintly perfumed flavour; sharper at picking and mellower after storage. Grown more for looks, cooking and coloured juice than for depth of flavour.

name: Gloster
summary: Firm, crisp and juicy greenish-cream flesh with a fairly sharp flavour, tarter than Delicious, finishing with a hint of honey according to one grower. Hangs well on the tree, keeps its crunch for months and mellows slightly in store.

name: Golden Russet
aka: Golden Russet of Western New York
summary: Dense, fine-grained, crisp flesh with intense sugar balanced by lively acidity; nutty and rich, with some tasters noting a hint of pear and a spiced, cider-like depth. Sharp early in the season, it sweetens markedly in store but loses crispness after a month or two.
best_eaten: Nov-Feb; sweeter after a few weeks in store

name: Greensleeves
summary: Crisp and juicy with a clean, refreshing tang when picked early; it mellows to a milder, sweeter apple in store.

name: Haralson
summary: Firm, crisp and juicy with a distinctly tart, fairly complex flavour that mellows a little in store. Holds its shape when baked, which made it the Upper Midwest's standard pie apple.
best_eaten: Oct-Feb; tart at picking, more balanced after a month or two in store

name: Hidden Rose
summary: Very firm, crisp, juicy red flesh with a bright sweet-tart balance and fruity berry and citrus notes; quite sharp if picked early, sweeter after a few weeks, and it can last into February. Flavour depends on site: one grower found it never developed real flavour at a research station.

name: Hyslop
summary: Firm yellow flesh, juicy at first but soon mealy, with a mildly acid and distinctly astringent flavour. Used for jelly, pickling and cider blends rather than eating raw.
best_eaten: Soon after picking, for jelly or pickling

name: Jester
summary: Crisp to softish, very juicy white flesh with a sweet, light flavour and little sharpness. Pleasant and refreshing rather than complex, and popular with children.

name: Kaiser Wilhelm
summary: Sweet-sharp with a distinctive raspberry-like aroma; firm and juicy when first picked but becoming drier and somewhat mealy as it stores.

name: Kerry Pippin
summary: Hard, very crisp yellowish flesh with a brisk, sugary and aromatic flavour of the sub-acid type. Older writers found it very juicy, while the National Fruit Collection describes it as rather dry. Best eaten soon after picking.

name: Kronprinz Rudolf
summary: Very juicy, fine and fairly soft white-to-cream flesh; sweet with a light, refreshing tartness and a delicate spicy perfume.

name: Lane's Prince Albert
summary: Very juicy, soft white flesh with a strong, clean acidity. It cooks to a sharp puree that keeps a little texture, and it softens and sweetens somewhat in store; flesh browns quickly once cut.

name: Limbertwig
summary: Firm to hard, yellowish, aromatic flesh with a distinctive flavour that improves in storage; Limbertwigs are valued more as long keepers and for pies, jelly and cider than as showy dessert apples. Flavour differs from strain to strain.

name: Lord Grosvenor
summary: Soft, white, juicy flesh with a clean, sharp acidity. A codlin-type cooker for late summer, used straight from the tree.
best_eaten: Aug-Sep, for cooking soon after picking

name: Maigold
summary: Crunchy, firm, fine-grained and juicy, with a sweet but balanced flavour and honeyed, pear-like notes; tasters report a citrus edge appearing as it keeps. Bruises less readily than most.

name: Melba
summary: Snow-white, crisp and juicy flesh that softens fairly quickly, with a sweet, lightly tart, wine-like flavour and the perfumed skin aroma typical of the McIntosh family. Also makes good sauce.
best_eaten: Aug-early Sep; eat soon after picking or use for sauce

name: Miller's Seedling
summary: White, very juicy flesh, crisp but light when first picked and soon softening, with a sweet, refreshingly tart and fragrant flavour. It bruises at the slightest knock and goes waxy within about a week, so eat it straight from the tree.
best_eaten: Late Aug-mid Sep, fresh from the tree

name: Nonpareil
summary: One of the small group of pear-drop apples: a strong pear-drop flavour with lively, wine-like acidity and an aftertaste some growers liken to honey and pear. Growers disagree on texture, some finding the flesh soft and sponge-like with modest juice, others surprisingly juicy. Best kept until mid-winter, when it sweetens.

name: Nuvar Golden Hills
summary: Crisp and juicy with a sweet, fairly rich flavour; a little sweeter than its Greensleeves parent.

name: Palmer's Rosey
summary: Crisp, fairly tender flesh with a noticeably aromatic flavour for an August apple.
best_eaten: Late Aug-Sep, straight from the tree

name: Pig's Nose Pippin
summary: Fine-grained, crisp cream flesh with a sweet flavour. Few other tasting details are recorded.

name: Polly
summary: Soft white flesh with a sweet, gently acidic flavour; usable both raw and in the kitchen.

name: Pristine
summary: Crisp, juicy, firm yellow flesh that is Granny Smith-tart if picked a few weeks early, mellowing at full ripeness to a gentle tartness with sweetness beneath; one grower notes a pear-like flavour with a citrus bite. Unusually good for such an early apple but best eaten within a week or two; also good for sauce.
best_eaten: Aug, within a week or two of picking

name: Red Astrachan
summary: Juicy, crisp white flesh, often tinged red, with a brisk tart flavour and some aroma. Good eaten straight from the tree but goes mealy within days; best known as a sauce and pie apple.
best_eaten: Aug, within a few days of picking

name: Red Windsor
summary: Crisp, very juicy, firm yellowish flesh with an aromatic, Cox-like flavour that is tangier and cleaner-tasting than Cox; most tasters find it refreshingly sharp, and it gains a honeyed sweetness only when fully ripe. A short keeper, best eaten within a week or so of picking.
best_eaten: Sep-Oct, within a few weeks of picking

name: Ribston Pippin
summary: Firm, fine-grained flesh with a strong, aromatic flavour that is more robust, if less refined, than its offspring Cox; sources note a pear-like taste and one grower a pronounced lemon tang. At its best about a month after picking, but it does not stay crisp for long and browns quickly when cut.
best_eaten: Oct-Jan; best after a month in store

name: Royal Jubilee
summary: Firm, yellow, medium-coarse flesh with a moderate sub-acid taste. A sound cooker of no special aroma.

name: Sansa
summary: Essentially an early Gala: sweet, juicy and crisp, but with more acidity from Akane to keep it lively. Eat within a week or so of picking; late fruit can turn grainy.

name: Self-Fertile Cox
summary: Tastes like Cox's Orange Pippin: rich and aromatic with honeyed sweetness, floral and pear-drop notes and balancing acidity. Some growers find heavy self-set crops give smaller fruit with slightly less depth.
best_eaten: Oct-Dec; flavour peaks a few weeks after picking

name: Sima Joon
summary: A crisp late apple whose flavour is described as an even balance of sweetness and acidity. Early reports only; it has had very little independent tasting.

name: Spartan
summary: Snow-white, crisp, juicy flesh with a sweet, vinous McIntosh character and a light perfume; tasters variously note hints of melon and strawberry or a burnt-caramel, toffee-apple tone. Best straight off the tree: it softens within a week or so, browns quickly when cut, and long-stored fruit can taste fermented.

name: Sturmer Pippin
summary: Very firm, crisp and juicy. Hard and sharp when first picked, it slowly sweetens in store and by late winter is rich and brisk, still with plenty of acidity.
best_eaten: Jan-Apr; not worth eating before midwinter

name: Sweet Coppin
summary: A pure sweet: sugary juice with very little acid or tannin, used to soften sharper or more tannic fruit in a blend.
best_eaten: Not for eating; mill soon after picking in Nov.

name: Tom Putt
summary: Sharp and juicy with a slightly bitter edge when picked, mellowing into a brisk, fragrant eating apple after a few weeks. It cooks well and makes a sharp cider with low tannin.
best_eaten: Sep-Nov; cook or press from picking, eat fresh once it has mellowed

name: Tropical Beauty
summary: Sold as a sweet-tart eating apple for warm climates; reliable independent tasting notes were not found.

name: Warner's King
summary: Juicy, rather soft and coarse greenish flesh with a very sharp acidity. Breaks down quickly into a tart puree when cooked.

name: William Crump
summary: Firm, fine-textured and juicy, with plenty of sweetness and an intense, rich aromatic flavour drawn from its Cox parent.

name: Worcester Pearmain
summary: Firm, crisp white flesh that is sweet rather than sharp, with the well-known strawberry-like, slightly perfumed flavour, though its intensity varies. Traditional advice is to let it ripen fully on the tree because early-picked fruit is dull, yet some growers prefer it just short of full ripeness since ripe fruit softens fast; either way it keeps only about a week.
best_eaten: Sep-early Oct; leave on the tree until fully coloured

name: Yellow Ingestrie
summary: Fine-textured, tender flesh with an intense, rich sweet-sharp and pleasantly aromatic flavour; one taster found a hint of pineapple. Only moderately juicy, and best eaten within two or three weeks of its early-September picking.
